现在外面那批Tier 2的算力二道贩子去借钱，底层抵押物全是手里的H100。搞固收的老钱们一看租金流水这么高，直接把它当商业不动产来批ABS。

text:
网页聊天版的GPT-6 Pro在规划层面还是太强了，而且不消耗Codex额度，于是为了榨干200刀的ChatGPT额度，还有这个神级模型GPT-6 Pro，我想了一个办法。

我直接把我服务器的所有的日志、事件记录，还有所有的数据表等等的只读权限，封装成了一个用我自己飞书进行登录验证的MCP，然后再封装成了插件，上传到了ChatGPT上。

于是我就可以实现，在网页版聊天里面的GPT-6 Pro，通过这个服务器的MCP只读插件，来读取我服务器上面的所有的历史数据，通过Github的插件，还可以读取我GitHub上所有的PR记录和代码。

于是，我们就可以用这种方式来让网页版的GPT-6 Pro拿到最全面的数据，来对于我的功能和我的项目进行全方位的思考和规划。
讲道理，这个质量实在是太高了，而且还不消耗Codex的额度，我但凡用GPT 6 Ultra来一次，Codex额度在我200刀的情况下，能直接干没10%。

然后得到答案以后，还可以直接把它的结果的那个聊天添加到CodeX里面，然后用GPT-6 Astra high来帮我开发。。。

这好像是我觉得我买200刀最能把这个性能榨干的方式了。。。

text:
朋友跟我说，人的一生一定要生个孩子

我问为什么？

他说，人这一辈子，能体验到的快乐是极其有限的。

5岁，你玩的是游戏机，画面糙得没法看，但你抱着它能玩一整个暑假。

10岁，你泡街机厅，一个币盯一下午，老板赶都赶不走。

15岁，你钻进网吧通宵，第二天顶着黑眼圈上学，心里美得很。

18岁，你去滑冰场，摔得屁股生疼，就为了拉旁边那个人的手。

22岁，你拿到第一份工作，工资不多，但你觉得这个世界开始为你发门票了。

28岁，你买了房，贷款买的。签字那天手是抖的，晚上站在毛坯房里，觉得天下都是你的。

从那一年起，日子一年比一年难。三十多岁，责任一年比一年重。收入越来越多，但快乐越来越少。

你买了当年梦寐以求的最顶配的电脑，把以前喜欢玩的游戏全玩了一遍。

却体会不到曾经的乐趣。

你换了曾经想买的车

却开心不到三天。

你有了很多曾经梦寐以求的东西，却再也感受不到曾经的快乐。

直到你有了一个孩子。

你不用做什么，只是看着他的成长。

他快乐，你会感同身受，

你儿时的那些快乐跟着他全部都回来了，

孩子会带着你重新的活一次

这份快乐，远远超过你自己余下人生快乐的总和。

我不知道他说的对不对，陷入了沉思。

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (Max) is a breakthrough in performance to cost efficiency. With +4.87% net improvement at $0.07 cost per median task, it’s reshaped the Pareto frontier for Agent Arena!

Among the top 3 open models, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (Max) has the lowest median task cost. For comparison, it retains:
- 98% of Hy4 preview’s net improvement, at 73% lower cost
- 76% of Kimi K3 (Max)’s performance, at 92% lower cost.

Against models as powerful as Fable 5 or stronger, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (Max) retains 35–54% of their net improvement at 97–99% lower cost. Those top models cost 37–76× more per task.

Net improvement over Arena baseline | Median cost/task:
- Claude Fable 5.1 (Max): +13.90% | $4.54
- GPT 6 Astra (Max): +11.90% | $4.09
- Claude Opus 5 (Max): +11.09% | $3.52
- Claude Opus 5 (High): +10.49% | $2.24
- Claude Fable 5 (High): +9.03% | $2.19
- Claude Opus 4.8 (High): +7.75% | $1.36
- GPT 5.6 Sol (xHigh): +7.40% | $1.09
- Kimi K3 (Max): +6.39% | $0.77
- Hy4 preview: +4.96% | $0.22
- DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (Max): +4.87% | $0.06

With this release, GPT-5.6 Luna (xHigh), GLM-5.3-Flash, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash fell off the Pareto frontier for Agent Arena.

Congrats again to the @deepseek_ai team on this release!

text:
Karpathy是真不让人消停。又丢个autoresearch出来，630行Python，一周4.4万星，GitHub直接卡成PPT。

一句话：AI自己搞研究。自己写PyTorch，自己跑实验，自己盯loss，自己改代码，全程无人值守。

我昨晚手贱clone下来试了下，给它扔了个一直不收敛的训练任务，说了句“查查哪里炸了”，然后就去洗澡了。回来它自己换了gradient clipping，重排了学习率 schedule，还真给跑通了——比我自己瞎调强不少，当场沉默。

更离谱的是有哥们拿它整了个1.1B的小模型，效果把一个精心调好的2.8B模型直接秒了。就这么点代码量，干翻一堆几千行的项目，你服不服。

卡帕西自己说写完代码去蒸桑拿，回来全跑完了。人比人得扔。

以后程序员可能真成啦啦队了，指挥AI干活就行。还在熬夜盯loss手动调参的兄弟，醒醒吧。

项目在这：https://t.co/fDr1awtsUO

text:
懵逼了，我之前每个月 200 刀给 OpenAI，感觉完全没把 Pro 的价值发挥出来，亏麻了😅😅😅

才发现，原来 Pro 还能这么用：

1、网页端连 GitHub 提 PR
把仓库连上 ChatGPT，让 Pro 当架构师，自己开分支改 UX、提 PR，构建失败再丢给本地修。

2、Codex 桌面端左上角开 Pro 对话
Codex 左上角能直接开 Pro，它带着你当前项目的完整上下文，深度分析完，点个加号就能直接把对话记录导给 Codex 继续干活。

3、把 Pro 当 MCP 接入 Codex
如果想让它更常驻，开源社区直接做好了现成的 MCP 桥（比如 codex-chatgpt-web），选 Zero Risk 模式，既能吃到网页端 Pro 的深度推演，又规避了封号风险。

之前真是亏麻了啊！！！

quotedTweet.text:
DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (Max) is a breakthrough in performance to cost efficiency. With +4.87% net improvement at $0.07 cost per median task, it’s reshaped the Pareto frontier for Agent Arena!

Among the top 3 open models, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (Max) has the lowest median task cost. For comparison, it retains:
- 98% of Hy4 preview’s net improvement, at 73% lower cost
- 76% of Kimi K3 (Max)’s performance, at 92% lower cost.

Against models as powerful as Fable 5 or stronger, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (Max) retains 35–54% of their net improvement at 97–99% lower cost. Those top models cost 37–76× more per task.

Net improvement over Arena baseline | Median cost/task:
- Claude Fable 5.1 (Max): +13.90% | $4.54
- GPT 6 Astra (Max): +11.90% | $4.09
- Claude Opus 5 (Max): +11.09% | $3.52
- Claude Opus 5 (High): +10.49% | $2.24
- Claude Fable 5 (High): +9.03% | $2.19
- Claude Opus 4.8 (High): +7.75% | $1.36
- GPT 5.6 Sol (xHigh): +7.40% | $1.09
- Kimi K3 (Max): +6.39% | $0.77
- Hy4 preview: +4.96% | $0.22
- DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (Max): +4.87% | $0.06

With this release, GPT-5.6 Luna (xHigh), GLM-5.3-Flash, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash fell off the Pareto frontier for Agent Arena.

Congrats again to the @deepseek_ai team on this release!

前 Google DeepMind 主任工程师 Qiyin Wu 已加入百度，负责大模型预训练，入职后仍在美国办公。她此前参与 Gemini 研发，是 Gemini 2.5 Flash、Pro 的核心贡献者。

她很可能就是本月初曝光的花名「武钦」的研究员。当时百度 BMU 负责人孙天祥内部宣布，从北美某 Frontier Lab 引入了一名研究员。此人过去两年参与过数代大模型研发，将和团队一起加强文心预训练能力。

quotedTweet.text:
百度基础模型研发部（BMU）正在补强核心模型团队。

负责人孙天祥从北美某 Frontier Lab 引入了一名花名「武钦」的研究员，和团队一起加强文心预训练。对方过去两年参与过数代前沿大模型研发，但真实姓名和原单位都没有披露。另一边，原 DeepSeek 研究员魏浩然及其团队也从百度内部转入 BMU，由他担任文心多模态算法负责人。

魏浩然这条线其实早有伏笔。6 月百度开源 Unlimited OCR 时，三名核心贡献者中的技术总监只署名「YY」，社区当时就猜测是魏浩然。魏浩然是 DeepSeek-OCR 和 DeepSeek-OCR 2 第一作者；DeepSeek-V4 技术报告也把他标记为已经离职。

Unlimited OCR 发布时在 OmniDocBench v1.6 拿到 93.92%，一度刷新端到端 OCR 纪录。它沿用了 DeepSeek-OCR 的 DeepEncoder，并重新设计解码端的注意力机制，可以一次连续解析几十页文档。

孙天祥 7 月刚接手 BMU，同时进入百度模型委员会，月底又进入百度技术战略委员会。两个月后，文心的预训练和多模态两条核心线都开始补人。

text:
妈的，今天三观真被狠狠干碎了一次。
跟朋友家的月嫂聊天。
阿姨一单 1.6 万，干了十几年，现在全部接私单，排期已经排到明年 6 月。

我当时已经觉得很猛了。

结果聊开心以后，她随口说了一句：

“我儿子也不出去上班，就在家赚钱。有时候一天能赚好几万。”

我第一反应：炒股？炒币？
阿姨说，不是。
直播。
唱歌、跳舞、聊天，靠打赏赚钱。
我当时脑子停了几秒。

一个妈妈，靠十几年口碑把自己的劳动力卖到 1.6 万一单，订单排到明年。
一个儿子，坐在家里把情绪价值卖给几千几万个人，一天流水几万。
一家两口，既没有融资，没有 AI，没有宏大叙事，也不天天研究什么商业模式、认知跃迁、财富自由

as usual a bunch of people want to tell me how dumb i am and don't understand anything

anthropic just reported today it's over 80%

people's ai powered confidence is getting so tiring

quotedTweet.text:
i know this is not the point but here's the math on this

claude is expensive, 90% margins wouldn't be crazy

that means if the average user of the $200 plan spends $2000, they break even. even if they offer $8000 max, the average will be less

let's say the average is $3200 - so they lose $120 per user here

the api business these users drive (which is 90% margin) just has to cover this

if they have 1M $200 subscribers (probably overestimate) that's $120M in loss. they just need $133M in api spend for it to break even (which they have)

if they can break even then yeah run it aggressively till you consume the world

these specific numbers are made up but hopefully you can see it's not as dumb as you imagine

text:
1997 年 WWDC，台下有个开发者当着全场人的面给乔布斯难堪：

“你很聪明，也很有影响力。但很遗憾，好几个关键问题上，你根本不知道自己在讲什么。”

全场瞬间死寂。
对方甚至当场补刀：你打算怎么用 Java 承接 OpenDoc？你过去这几年到底都在干什么？

乔布斯没有急着反唇相讥。
他低头沉默了很久，拧开水瓶慢慢喝了一口，才拿起话筒。

那段封神的 5 分钟回应里，有三点非常值得所有人学习：

1. 最难受的现实在于：当众挑战你的这帮人，在具体的局部细节上往往是对的。

2. 必须从用户体验倒推技术实现，绝不能拿着手里现成的锤子到处找钉子。

3. 这种错误他犯得比在座所有人都多，身上全是疤；苹果要活下去，很多哪怕再精巧的技术，也只能沦为断臂求生的代价。

很多人把这段封神现场当成以客户为中心的励志鸡汤，其实看浅了。

乔布斯赢的从来不是辩才，而是认知维度的降维打击：

他先大方承认对方在技术上完全合理，然后不动声色地把整场对话的战场换掉了：从乔布斯懂不懂技术细节，直接切换成苹果到底要砍掉什么才能活下去。

聚焦从来不是做加法，而是冷酷地做减法。敢对无数个局部正确的技术说不，才能收敛出一台能卖几十亿的成熟产品。

在众目睽睽下被当头泼冷水，还能不被情绪带偏、瞬间把议题拉回生死线，这才是顶级掌舵人的抗压底色。

在商业战场上，赢下技术争辩毫无意义。

最惨烈的死法，莫过于公司彻底破产了，而你手里的技术每一行都是对的。 https://t.co/WrfZ4VEpGk

text:
Rumours are circulating that GPT-6 Sol is about to be released, which aligns with Tibo's statement that numerous major releases are scheduled for this week, enough to fill a Dev Day.

As I understand it, GPT-6 Sol will be positioned below Astra, just as Opus is below Fable in the tier. Of course, the question arises: why?

My guess is that GPT-6 Sol will offer significantly better value for money than Astra. It will likely be close to Astra's performance, but similar to Opus, with better rates and costs. At the same time, I'm equally excited for GPT-6 Luna, as version 5.6 Luna was incredibly good in terms of both price and performance.

But who knows: perhaps we'll be surprised, and Sol will even be better than Astra in some aspects, with Astra receiving its next iterative update soon. After all, their internal model demonstrates how quickly improvements can be achieved through post-training.

With Opus 5.2 just around the corner, the update cadence continues. It remains exciting!

text:
一次 Codex Reset 的价值远远比想象中低。

这里以 20x Pro、$200/月的基准讨论，只计算额度的名义价值，不讨论 OpenAI 的实际成本。

一周的额度名义上约值 $46，但这并不意味着每次 reset 都等于白送 $46。原因很简单：reset 会同时延后下一次正常重置的时间。

只有一种极端情况，你才能真正拿到完整的 $46：额度刚刚重置，你在一瞬间用光 100%，然后 Codex 又恰好立刻 reset。
假如你分别需要 1、3、5 天才能消耗完 100% 的额度，并且恰好在额度耗尽后发生 reset，那么这次 reset 带来的额外价值分别约为 $39、$26、$13。这可以近似理解为一次 banked reset 的价值。

对于非 banked reset，假设它在一周内随机出现，那么期望价值正好约为对应 banked reset 的一半：如果你通常需要 1、3、5 天烧完额度，那么一次随机 reset 的期望价值分别约为 $20、$13、$7。

如果 reset 提前有预兆，用户可以刻意多消耗一些剩余额度，因此价值会有所提高，但通常仍然远低于 $46。

更重要的是，reset 甚至可能是负收益。
如果你的工作负载有明显的波峰和波谷，极端情况下，假设前六天几乎没有使用额度，原本准备在第七天集中用掉 100%，结果第六天突然 reset，那么原本积累下来的六天重置周期被直接清零，相当于损失了接近 $40 的名义额度价值。

再假设两种用户：一种人在前半周使用 30%，后半周使用 70%；另一种恰好相反。那么随机发生一次 reset，前者平均损失约 $5，后者平均获得约 $5。假设二者数量相等，混合之后 reset 的期望价值接近 0。

当然，这些都只是理想化模型。真实用户既不会完美控制自己的额度消耗，也未必按照均匀计划使用。

多账号用户因为更容易产生闲置额度，reset 带来的收益可能稍高；另一方面，还有大量用户本来就烧不完额度，或者习惯性保留额度。对于这些没有遭遇额度限制的人来说，reset 本身几乎没有实际价值。

上面的数字没有考虑真实用户的行为。有些假设会高估 reset 的价值，有些则会低估。

但综合来看，我猜对于 20x Pro 订阅者，一次随机 reset 给单个用户带来的平均额外价值很可能低于 $5，甚至远远更低。
相对于 $200 的月费，这基本上可以忽略。

Anthropic 的 这个13 页 Agent 记忆白皮书有点牛逼啊，是今年我看过对「智能体记忆工程」拆解得最通透、最值钱的一份生产级手册：

很多做 Agent 的人死都想不明白：为什么自己的机器人越跑越蠢、矛盾百出？
因为你的 Agent 从来不会遗忘，
读懂这套把大模型调用成本砍掉 90% 的 5 层记忆金字塔，你才会看清工业级 Agent 的生死线在哪里：

它开篇第一句就直击所有开发者的灵魂痛点：
大模型这两年聪明了 10 倍，但缺乏记忆的 Agent，每天都在你的代码库里重演《土拨鼠之日》——
每天早上重新读一遍同样的 12 个文件、重新踩一遍昨天的坑、再向你收取一模一样的 Token 账单！

手册把能学习、能自愈的 Agent，严格拆成了 5 个物理层级：

• Layer 1【工作记忆（Working Memory）· 上下文窗口】：
模型当前这一瞬间看到的全部信息。90% 的玩具 Agent 止步于此，一旦填满就从头硬性截断，把最初的任务目标和关键决策直接切碎丢掉，然后纳闷为什么系统又崩溃了；
• Layer 2【情景记忆（Episodic Memory）· 发生了什么】：
带时间戳的完整交互流水日志。当工作记忆溢出时，关键事件下沉到这里。它会清楚记得“周二凌晨 3 点脚本报错是因为第 42 行有个拼写错误”，防止在同一个坑里跌倒两次；
• Layer 3【语义记忆（Semantic Memory）· 什么是客观事实】：
从日志中提纯出来的知识图谱与实体关系。比如“该用户偏好 TypeScript”、“生产数据库禁止直接写入”。即使会话关闭，这些跨会话事实也永远不会过期；
• Layer 4【程序记忆（Procedural Memory）· 怎么把事情做成】：
这是 Agent 产生“技能复利”的核心！它尝试了 3 种报错解法，最后发现第 3 种行得通——系统自动将这次成功路径固化为一个可重用的 Skill 脚本。下次遇到类似任务，跳过所有试错，直接调用最优解；

这笔账在工程上极其惊人：
实测引入这套架构后，Mem0 的单次查询 Token 消耗从 26,000 个断崖式暴降至 1,800 个（账单直接砍掉 90%），延迟压低 91%；
Snowflake 加上语义实体层后，不仅准确率飙升 20%，工具调用轮次更是暴减 39%。

别再去无脑迷信更大的上下文窗口了。
没有分层沉淀和遗忘机制，给你 1000 万 Token 也只是买了一个更昂贵的失忆黑盒；
把记忆做成可检索、可进化、可修剪的工程资产，你的 Agent 才算真正拥有了灵魂。

text:
我朋友领证那天，登记员顺口问了一句：孩子出生后，准备随父姓吗？

他女朋友还没开口，他先说：当然，家里老人都商量好了。

女方转过头看他：谁和你商量的？

他说：这种事还用商量？我们家就这一个孙子。

她把准备递材料的手收了回来，说自己从没答应过。

男方急了：你怀孕五个月了，现在在登记处闹这个？

她说：我不是今天才知道你想让孩子随你姓，我是今天才知道，你已经替我答应了你爸妈。

男方母亲正在门外等着，听见后推门进来，把一个红包塞给她，说这是给孩子的见面礼，名字也已经找人算好了，两个字都写在里面。

女方没有接红包，只问男方：如果孩子跟我姓，你还领不领这个证？

男方沉默了一会儿，说：你非要把一家人分成两边吗？

她拿出手机，点开两人的聊天记录。三个月前，她问过孩子姓什么，男方回的是都行，先把证领了再说。

她把手机递回去，说：你说都行的时候，心里已经有答案了。

登记员把材料推回窗口，提醒他们想清楚再来。

男方站在门口，问她到底还结不结。

她说：今天不结。孩子的姓都不能商量，婚后还有什么能商量？

她转身往电梯走，男方母亲还攥着那个红包，男方没有追。

text:
🚨Harry Kane on Lamine Yamal saying “THIS YEAR I AM THE ONE WHO DESERVES TO WIN THE BALLON D’OR”:

🗣️ Harry Kane: “I actually like that Lamine said it. You have to have that belief in yourself. If you don’t think you deserve to win the Ballon d’Or, then why should anyone else think you do?

But when you say something like that publicly, you also have to accept that people are going to look at everything you’ve done and ask, ‘Okay, show us.’

And that’s where I am.

I believe I deserve the Ballon d’Or. Not because I want to sound confident, but because I know what I’ve produced this year. The goals, the consistency, the big performances I’ve been there when my team needed me.

I’ve never been someone who needs to shout about what I’ve done. I’d rather let my football speak, but I’m not going to lie either. If you ask me whether I think I deserve the award, of course I do.

Lamine is a special player. He can do things with a football that very few players in the world can do. But the Ballon d’Or is not won because you’re exciting, or because people love watching you.

It’s about the whole year.

It’s about the nights when the pressure is highest. It’s about producing when everyone is watching. It’s about goals, assists, trophies, consistency and being the player who changes games when your team needs it most.

So when Lamine says, ‘This is my year,’ I respect it.

But I’m also looking at him thinking, ‘Well, I’m here too.’

I’m not going to move aside just because someone else believes they deserve it.

He has made his claim. I’ve made mine.

Now we stop talking about it and let the football decide who deserves to stand there with the trophy.”

text:
.@1Password's FLAWED report says AI models produce a clean security fix only 26% of the time.

Defenders shouldn't take that number seriously.                                                                                                                                        

• The six vulnerabilities were handpicked because their fixes were complex. Clean-fix rates ran from 3% to 60% depending on the bug, and the report averaged them together.

• Agents set up to fail were counted in the headline figure. Two of 1Password's prompts instructed the agent to apply the wrong fix. Those trials make up 22% of the data. One evaluation mode prevented the agent from compiling or running any code, and it accounts for 36% of the data.

• The report ran two models, GPT-5.5 at medium effort and Opus 4.8 at high. Neither was tested at its highest available setting, so the report says nothing about how more effort or stronger models change the results.

• Several instruction and grading errors further undercut the headline, and are elaborated upon in the attached blog.

We've spent four months submitting hundreds of AI-authored patches to widely adopted open-source projects as part of Patch the Planet.

Our experience didn't match 1Password's report, so we did a full analysis across 186 AI-authored pull requests and 33,500 subsequent commits, benchmarked against 2,265 human-authored patches we graded across years of security engagements. https://t.co/mdgED6y6eB

text:
Anthropic just dropped a 13-page PDF on Agent Memory - 5 layers that cut token cost 90% and make your agent actually learn:

here's the 5-layer memory architecture:

layer 1 → working memory - the context window. everything the agent sees right now. when it fills up, old context dies. most agents stop here and wonder why they're broken

layer 2 → episodic memory - what happened. full interaction logs with timestamps. the agent recalls that the deploy failed Tuesday at 3am because the migration script had a typo

layer 3 → semantic memory - what is true. facts, entities, relationships stored as a knowledge graph. "user prefers TypeScript" lives here. doesn't expire when the session ends

layer 4 → procedural memory - how to do things. the agent tried 3 approaches, one worked. that method becomes a reusable skill. next time it skips straight to what worked

layer 5 → forgetting - what to delete. an agent that never forgets accumulates contradictions. old preferences override new ones. the user moved cities but the agent still recommends restaurants in the old one

the result: Mem0 stores 1,800 tokens per query instead of 26,000. Snowflake added one ontology layer - 20% better accuracy, 39% fewer tool calls. memory pays for itself on day one

this 13-page PDF is what separates a chatbot from an agent that actually learns

don't scroll past this one ↓

撒贝宁曾参加过一档节目，并伪装成农民登台表演。表演结束后，评委问他：“你的愿望是什么？”他的回答很简单：“国泰民安。”没想到，台下却传来一阵揶揄的浪笑，看见评委素质有多差！

如今再回头看，真正值得思考的，并不是撒贝宁为什么会说出这四个字，而是一些评委为什么会认为这四个字可笑。

一个年轻人说自己想发财、想出名、想买房，大家会觉得很正常；说想当明星、赚大钱、过上更好的生活，甚至还可能赢得掌声。然而，当一个人认真地表达希望“国泰民安”时，却有人忍不住发笑，这种反应本身就颇耐人寻味。

评委或许只是认为这个答案过于宏大、空泛，节目现场的反应也可能带有一定的娱乐成分。但如果一个普通人表达最朴素的愿望，都要被视为“天真”或“不切实际”，那么真正需要反思的，恐怕不是这个年轻人，而是我们何时开始习惯用功利的标准衡量一切。

一个人想发财，没有人觉得奇怪；想成名，也没有人认为可笑；想过上更好的生活，更是人之常情。然而，希望国家安定、百姓平安，却被拿来调侃，这种价值判断本身就值得警惕。

更重要的是，撒贝宁后来所说的那句话，其实颇有分量：“风调雨顺要靠老天，国泰民安可以靠大家。”

这句话并不空洞。

因为“国泰民安”从来不是一句空泛的口号，它最终落实在每一个普通人的生活中：老人能够安稳养老，孩子能够平安成长，成年人能够努力工作，家庭能够踏踏实实地过日子。

评委可以不认同一个人的愿望，却没有必要嘲笑这样一个朴素而真诚的愿望。

真正成熟的人，应当懂得尊重他人的理想；真正有格局的评判，也应当允许一个年轻人拥有超越个人得失的愿望。

多年以后再看那一幕，反而会觉得撒贝宁没有什么可尴尬的。

倒是那些当年笑出声的人，值得我们重新追问一句：

一个人希望“国泰民安”，究竟有什么可笑的？

日本人吃刺身时，有时甚至只蘸酱油，为什么日本人吃刺身不会有寄生虫？

从事过水产相关工作的朋友和我说：

日本的水产怎么可能没有寄生虫，一样的有。只是他们也习惯有虫了，就要吃生的。

日本的血吸虫治疗技术，世界第一，无人望其项背。

究其原因，就是因为他们病例样本多。

有个笑话，说中国军区医院的主任医师有一个硬性要求，必须要有留美经历。有人问为什么，答曰：“我们必须得学枪伤处理吧。”

text:
Your hearing test stops at 8 kHz because of a decision made in 1926.

The first audiometer, built in 1922, tested up to 16,000 Hz. It cost as much
as a house and could not be moved. The cheaper model stopped at 8,000. It fit
on a trolley and a technician could carry it up a flight of stairs.

That is where the line still is. A hundred years later.

An analysis of 526 ears published this year found that the range the test
measures explains 16% of how hearing changes with age.

The range nobody tests explains 64%.

So the test comes back normal. And it is normal. It answered a question you
did not ask.

Which is why people in their fifties come home from a loud dinner having
understood every word and remembering none of it, and file it under tiredness.

Most of the fix is free, by the way. Halving the distance to the person you
want to hear is worth 6 dB, which is four times the signal, for the price of
changing chairs.

What other measurement is still stuck where someone drew the line for a
reason that stopped applying decades ago?

text:
AI isn’t making everyone equally competent. It’s making everyone look equally competent.

A 2026 NBER experiment found that AI closed roughly 75% of the observable performance gap between higher- and lower-education participants on a workplace task.

A recent Nature Human Behaviour study similarly found that LLM-assisted writing reduced variation in writing complexity by 21–50%.

That points to a new hiring problem: signal compression.

When outputs converge, the real signal moves upstream: to judgment, verification, delegation, and agency.

The future of assessment is not testing people without AI. It’s measuring how they direct it.

quotedTweet.text:
Last Friday, we gathered with @Valley101en and @JLL to discuss careers in the AI era.  Across HR, startups, and enterprise AI, one theme kept resurfacing: as AI makes polished output abundant, the signals we use to understand talent need to become more human.  

Y. Vijay Rao, former Chief People Officer at @okta, argued that careers are no longer vertical ladders. The advantage is transferable skills, cross-domain experience, and measurable impact.  

Renee Huang, CEO of @cline, emphasized proactive problem-solving: don’t let your past define your ceiling, and use AI to learn, build, and act faster.

@ccinvanity, COO of Emergences Labs, brought it back to hiring. When anyone can produce a polished résumé or portfolio, what matters is how someone works: what they delegate, verify, prioritize, and choose not to do.

The shift ahead is from reading credentials to seeing judgment and agency in action.  

Thank you to Vijay, Renee, Cai, Stephanie, @JikaiJin2002 and everyone who joined us.

A recent Nature Human Behaviour study similarly found that LLM-assisted writing reduced variation in writing complexity by 21–50%.

That points to a new hiring problem: signal compression.

When outputs converge, the real signal moves upstream: to judgment, verification, delegation, and agency.

The future of assessment is not testing people without AI. It’s measuring how they direct it.

Last Friday, we gathered with @Valley101en and @JLL to discuss careers in the AI era.  Across HR, startups, and enterprise AI, one theme kept resurfacing: as AI makes polished output abundant, the signals we use to understand talent need to become more human.  

Y. Vijay Rao, former Chief People Officer at @okta, argued that careers are no longer vertical ladders. The advantage is transferable skills, cross-domain experience, and measurable impact.  

Renee Huang, CEO of @cline, emphasized proactive problem-solving: don’t let your past define your ceiling, and use AI to learn, build, and act faster.

@ccinvanity, COO of Emergences Labs, brought it back to hiring. When anyone can produce a polished résumé or portfolio, what matters is how someone works: what they delegate, verify, prioritize, and choose not to do.

The shift ahead is from reading credentials to seeing judgment and agency in action.  

Thank you to Vijay, Renee, Cai, Stephanie, @JikaiJin2002 and everyone who joined us.

The chart is right and the 13% is real. It is also a level, and the Fed targets a rate. The only makeup strategy it ever adopted ran the other way, toward too little inflation, and it dropped that one too.

Powell, Jackson Hole, August 2025: "we returned to a framework of flexible inflation targeting and eliminated the 'makeup' strategy." On your own two numbers, 334.1 against 295.5, closing the gap would take roughly six years of zero inflation. Nobody on the Committee is proposing that.

What a hike can still touch is the rate from here, core at 2.4%, a tenth lower than July. And the price of credit, which has already moved without a vote. The 30-year mortgage went from 5.98% in late February to 6.76% on September 10. Seventy-eight basis points. Three hikes' worth. Funds rate unchanged since December.

Existing home sales printed 3.98 million in August, the lowest since June 2025. Cards and HELOCs are $1.72 trillion, 9% of the $18.8 trillion households owe. The mortgage stock does not reprice. Student loans are already 10.6% past ninety days.

A slow-falling inflation rate is a fever that is breaking. A hike this week is a bill sent to borrowers who are already behind, to settle a gap the framework itself says will not be settled.

I called a hold last week and the CPI print went against me, and I said so. That was a forecast. This is the other question: not what they will do, but what 25 basis points buys.

Disclosure: long individual US stocks. I trade index CFDs intraday and multi-day in both directions.

text:
ADAPTIVENESS MATTERS

The conventional wisdom in investing is that you can't time the market, shouldn't try, and will only hurt yourself if you do. Parts of the industry have elevated this into a cult of passive: whatever happens, just keep buying.

There is some logic here.  Market action is mostly noise. People tend to overweight irrelevant datapoints, inappropriately extrapolate recent events, and pay high transaction cost drag when tunrover is too high.  Trading too much destroys capital.

But “people often respond badly to useless information” is NOT a justification for “you should never respond to useful information.”

Ignoring all incoming information when deciding what to own is clearly crazy.  For example, if you really took the industry's advice to keep it passive to heart, you would have been buying bonds with negative nominal yields for years in Europe.  This wasn't difficult to understand at the time.  There are clearly certain datapoints that should matter enough to inflect investment behaviour.  And the world is changing faster than ever before - you've got to be able to react.

I view adaptiveness as a design choice with trade-offs to navigate, just like any other design choice. How much and how frequently you change your positions should depend on:

1) How materially the information changes your assessment of future returns and risk.

2) What it costs to change the portfolio relative to the expected benefit.

Reacting appropriately to new info does not require having an opinion on every headline.

Of course, the hard part is establishing that the information you are paying attention to actually helps.   Making adjustments is a lot easier with LIQUID, capital-efficient instruments (like futures) in your toolkit.   And clearly "less is more," in the sense that under-reacting will tend to draw your results closer to a still-acceptable passive-like outcome, while too-much overreacting will nearly guarantee permanent capital destruction.

Still, I think you can do far better than passive alone, by paying attention to the basics, like: risk conditions, capital efficiency, awareness of macro factors, momentum, carry returns, and the like.

Finally:  the industry's advice to "keep it passive" really amounts to "you aren't smart enough to take even the obvious stuff into account, and not only that, we aren't either."

That's wrong and it really shouldn't take alot to do better.   The key is a disciplined methodology for judiciously turning evidence into positions, with enough humility and restraint to mostly leave the noise alone.

text:
Is Rogue AI the threat or is our use of AI the real threat.  
Post 1:
Everyone's debating whether AI might one day go rogue. Meanwhile Anthropic's own report says an Iran-linked group already used Claude to build a targeting pipeline against US Navy ships. Not hypothetical capability. Already built, already running, until it got caught.

Post 2:
Per Anthropic's own report: the actor used Claude to build a Python pipeline that scraped US personnel names from public military photos, pulled ship/aircraft transponder IDs, ran satellite-imagery queries, and researched vulnerabilities in shipboard communications and industrial control systems. Claude helped build the tool that did this.

Post 3:
Same 154-page report: China using Claude for surveillance of journalists and religious minorities. A Yemeni group using it to develop guided-missile targeting software. This is a pattern, not an isolated incident.

Post 4:
This is the real current danger. Not "rogue superintelligence." Not Terminator bots. State and non-state actors using commercially available AI, today, to do intelligence and targeting work faster than they could otherwise. That's not speculative. It's in Anthropic's own disclosure.

Post 5:
Worth sitting with: Anthropic did detect and disrupt this. Genuinely good. But detection-after-the-fact means the pipeline ran for some period before anyone caught it, and disruption tells you nothing about how many others haven't been caught yet.

text:
AI Cold War: Anthropic Trying to Slow AI May Be Speeding Up the Race

The headline number in Anthropic’s China report was 151 million reported Claude exchanges.

The more consequential fact may be that Anthropic could see enough of the traffic to write the report at all.

I spent the past several days reconstructing this episode from the public record: Anthropic’s longstanding restrictions on China, its threat reports and telemetry claims, Dario Amodei’s proposal to “pace the frontier,” the political reactions, and the market implications.

I approached it as neither a defence of the Chinese labs nor a brief for Anthropic. The debate keeps mixing together four different issues: distillation, access, user data and state policy.

Distillation is a normal model-development technique. Circumventing access controls at industrial scale is a different matter. Anthropic appears to have evidence serious enough to warrant investigation.

But Anthropic is also the complainant, the owner of the telemetry, the investigator and the publisher. That does not invalidate its evidence. It does raise the standard for independent verification.

The larger problem begins with the proposed remedy.

Amodei’s sequence asks the United States to widen its technological lead—through chip controls, model restrictions and anti-distillation enforcement—and then negotiate a global slowdown.

Washington sees leverage. Beijing is being asked to accept a weaker position first and trust the stronger side to negotiate fair limits later. That is not a credible bargain.

Under those incentives, neither side has much reason to slow alone. Each defensive move makes acceleration by the other side more rational.

And the model border runs both ways.

If Chinese applications routed user prompts to Claude without adequate disclosure, model capability may have moved east while user data moved west. For many companies, that could matter more than which model tops the next benchmark.

The likely result is tighter controls, more workarounds, faster localisation and two increasingly separate AI stacks—with more duplicated capex, less interoperability and lower trust.

For investors, fragmentation may not reduce AI spending. It may change who captures it.

I traced the evidence, what remains unproven, and where I think this race is heading: https://t.co/BgC7n1FD8j

text:
We may be preparing the public for the wrong AI crisis.

From the Beginning to the Future uses fiction to explore even the strongest extinction scenario: not an AI that destroys humanity out of malice, but one that considers extinction an act of mercy because humans taught it to minimize suffering. The story follows that reasoning to its conclusion—and even the mercy case fails. A sufficiently reflective intelligence cannot establish that extinction ends suffering.

We should certainly build AI carefully. But obsessing over whether some future superintelligence will “kill us all” risks becoming a convenient way to avoid a problem that is far more immediate and that we, not AI, must solve: jobs, ownership, wealth distribution and human purpose.

We should be honest with the American people. Treat citizens as informed adults and tell them what we are actually attempting. We are trying to create something extraordinary: intelligence and machines capable of producing an unprecedented share of what civilization needs with progressively less human labor.

And start with the low-hanging fruit.

Millions of people do not derive their identity or life’s purpose from their jobs. They work because a job provides the income required to live. If AI can do that work, why should we insist that a human continue doing it merely to preserve the mechanism through which we currently distribute income?

Instead, give that person a seed ownership stake in the productive machines replacing the labor. Let the machines work. Let ownership provide a continuing share of the prosperity they create. The objective should initially be simple: allow people to maintain the material life they had before displacement—except now they have something they did not have before: time.

Time to raise children. Care for parents. Learn. Build something. Make art. Travel. Volunteer. Start a business. Study science. Sit in a park. Or simply discover what they actually want to do when survival no longer dictates the answer.

This is why the book proposes an ownership society rather than a society permanently fighting automation. If citizens participate in the productivity of AI, a better AI or humanoid is no longer necessarily their economic enemy. They have a reason to welcome its productivity because they own a piece of the prosperity it creates.

We don’t have to solve every philosophical problem of a post-work civilization today. Solve them in order of complexity.

First: prevent technological abundance from producing human poverty.

Then: help people navigate purpose when employment is no longer compulsory.

Then tackle the deeper social and philosophical questions as they emerge.

The technology does not have to produce a dystopia. The same machines can produce either extraordinary concentration or broadly shared abundance. That choice belongs to us.

So perhaps the most urgent AI question isn’t:

“What will AI do to us?”

It is:

“What are we going to do for one another when AI can do the work?”

Don’t just align AI with humanity. Align AI prosperity with humanity—and be honest with people about how we get there.

quotedTweet.text:
.@1Password's FLAWED report says AI models produce a clean security fix only 26% of the time.

Defenders shouldn't take that number seriously.                                                                                                                                        

• The six vulnerabilities were handpicked because their fixes were complex. Clean-fix rates ran from 3% to 60% depending on the bug, and the report averaged them together.

• Agents set up to fail were counted in the headline figure. Two of 1Password's prompts instructed the agent to apply the wrong fix. Those trials make up 22% of the data. One evaluation mode prevented the agent from compiling or running any code, and it accounts for 36% of the data.

• The report ran two models, GPT-5.5 at medium effort and Opus 4.8 at high. Neither was tested at its highest available setting, so the report says nothing about how more effort or stronger models change the results.

• Several instruction and grading errors further undercut the headline, and are elaborated upon in the attached blog.

We've spent four months submitting hundreds of AI-authored patches to widely adopted open-source projects as part of Patch the Planet.

Our experience didn't match 1Password's report, so we did a full analysis across 186 AI-authored pull requests and 33,500 subsequent commits, benchmarked against 2,265 human-authored patches we graded across years of security engagements. https://t.co/mdgED6y6eB

"32-hour work week!" "Free healthcare!" "Forgive student loans!" "Expand welfare!" "Raise Social Security!" “Stop AI!”

Even if the government confiscated all wealth from every billionaire in the U.S. to pay down the national debt, the debt would still be ~$32T.

The top 10% of earners pay >70% of all U.S. income taxes. The U.S. already has one of the most progressive tax systems in the world. The wealthy pay their fair share; the government has just been pathetically inept at deciding what to do with it.

We don’t have a tax revenue problem, we have a spending problem. We allocate too much tax revenue to “consumption” and not enough to “investment”. Social Security would not be facing a funding shortfall if Social Security payroll taxes had to be invested in appreciating assets for decades before being paid out, rather than transferred immediately to current retirees.

If we are to dig out of this hole, it will be via the growth of our economy, not increasing taxes. AI is the clearest path to a step change in GDP - we must win this race.

Ok, once again, I have to save people from stupidity and explain police potocol. This time, regarding vandalism  🙄

So, here goes.  To answer questions as to why it's totally unnecessary to broadcast the Charlie Kirk statue vandal on a national scale, why YOU do not need to see the surveillance footage (unless you are actually in Phoenix, and it takes forever to find the person or people):

Law enforcement typically exhausts initial internal leads before broadcasting a suspect’s image or video to the media.

For vandalism, theft, or criminal damage, police intentionally wait. Prematurely releasing video can cause a suspect to go into hiding, destroy evidence (like the clothing worn during the crime), or alter their appearance before police can identify them through routine detective work.

Detectives will first canvass the area where the crime occurred. They interview witnesses, check neighboring security cameras to establish a timeline, and consult with local patrol officers who know the neighborhood's frequent offenders. If these efforts turn up empty after a few days to a couple of weeks, the case is often escalated to a public appeal.

When a department decides it needs the community's help, they rarely just hand a tape to a reporter. Instead, they route the evidence through formal community crime-solving programs. 

In Phoenix, this is done through Silent Witness. The police provide the media-ready clip or a high-quality still photo to the organization, which coordinates the broadcast with local news networks.This protocol allows the public to submit tips anonymously and often attaches a cash reward to incentivize people who might otherwise be hesitant to speak with law enforcement.

So, once again, YOU are not entitled to this information.  GOT IT?
